title: TRACTION: A Hospital Policy of Tranexamic Acid in Major Noncardiac Surgery
breakthrough: TRACTION was a pragmatic, double-blind, cluster-randomised, placebo-controlled trial across 10 Canadian hospitals testing a hospital-wide POLICY of intraoperative tranexamic acid in major noncardiac surgery. More than 8,000 patients were included, of whom 5,002 (60.5%) underwent oncologic surgery. Red-cell transfusion occurred in 7.4% of the tranexamic acid group versus 9.8% with placebo. The rate of venous thromboembolism was similar between groups.
impact: The reservation about tranexamic acid in cancer surgery has always been thrombosis in an already hypercoagulable population. A trial in which three-fifths of patients had oncologic operations, showing a transfusion reduction with no VTE signal, removes the specific objection that kept it off standing order sets.
practical: The design is the point: this randomised a hospital POLICY by cluster, not individual patients, so what it supports is a default protocol rather than a case-by-case decision — which is how the drug actually gets given or missed. The absolute reduction is 2.4 percentage points, so the argument for it is cheapness and safety at scale, not a dramatic effect in any one patient. It does not license tranexamic acid where a specific contraindication exists, and the trial's follow-up for thrombotic events was 90 days.
link: TRACTION — hospital policy of tranexamic acid to reduce transfusion in major noncardiac surgery

verify.note: Fully verified and unusually accurate for this review. TRACTION, NEJM published 10 June 2026, 10 Canadian hospitals, more than 8,000 patients, 5,002 (60.5%) oncologic surgery, transfusion 7.4% versus 9.8%, VTE rates similar. The submission's numbers, journal, month and clinical conclusion all match the published trial. One clarification added, not a correction: it is a CLUSTER-randomised trial of a hospital policy, which strengthens rather than weakens the submission's 'universal perioperative TXA as a standard' framing, and is worth stating because it explains why the finding is about protocol design. The absolute risk difference has been stated alongside the relative claim.

title: BrIMA: Intraoperative Specimen PET-CT for Breast Margin Assessment
breakthrough: BrIMA was a prospective, multicentre, interventional NONRANDOMISED trial running June 2022 to March 2025 across six breast cancer centres in Belgium, Germany and Italy, analysing 148 patients undergoing breast-conserving surgery. Ten-minute specimen PET-CT performed in the operating room raised the intraoperative success rate in invasive ductal carcinoma from 83.3% without intraoperative margin assessment to 95.2% with it. Across all subtypes the rate rose from 76.4% to 91.9%. No device-related adverse events were reported.
impact: Positive margins are the leading reason a breast-conserving operation has to be repeated, and re-excision costs the patient a second anaesthetic, a delay to adjuvant therapy and a worse cosmetic result. Molecular imaging of the specimen while the patient is still asleep addresses the problem at the only moment it can be fixed without a second operation.
practical: Read the design before adopting: 148 patients, no randomised control arm, and the "without intraoperative margin assessment" comparator is derived from the same specimens rather than a separate group — so the 83.3%-to-95.2% figure is a within-specimen contrast, not a head-to-head. The study was conducted with a single commercial system (XEOS AURA 10) and the manufacturer publicised the result, which does not make it wrong but does mean independent replication and a cost-per-avoided-reoperation analysis are still owed. Ten minutes of added operative time per specimen is the resource question a unit has to answer.
link: BrIMA — specimen PET-CT imaging for intraoperative margin assessment in early-stage breast cancer

verify.status: corrected — numbers verified, but the trial is nonrandomised and the submission did not say so
verify.note: Verified: BrIMA, JAMA Surgery 2026, 148 patients, six centres in Belgium/Germany/Italy, June 2022–March 2025, IDC success 83.3% to 95.2%, all-subtype 76.4% to 91.9%, no device-related adverse events. The submission's headline figures are exactly right. Corrections are all about strength of evidence: (1) the published title says NONRANDOMIZED clinical trial, while the submission presents it as a 'Prospective Multicenter Trial' with no such qualifier; (2) the comparator is not a control group, so the improvement is a within-specimen contrast; (3) the submission omits that this is one commercial device (XEOS AURA 10) with a manufacturer press release, and omits the all-subtype figures, which are lower than the IDC ones it quoted. The submission's claim that this 'dramatically reduc[es] second-look procedures' is a reasonable inference but was not the measured endpoint — the endpoint was intraoperative success rate — so it has been reworded.

title: Metabolic Surgery Versus GLP-1 Therapy: Projected Cardiovascular Risk
breakthrough: A Mayo Clinic retrospective cohort of 812 adults with obesity compared one-year changes in ESTIMATED 10-year and lifetime atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease risk after metabolic and bariatric surgery (n=579) against GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy (n=233). Both treatments reduced estimated 10-year ASCVD risk. Projected LIFETIME ASCVD risk fell by 8.6% after surgery versus 1.7% with GLP-1 therapy, alongside mean total body weight loss of 28% versus 11%.
impact: It is the first direct comparison of the two dominant obesity treatments on a cardiovascular endpoint, and it separates them clearly in the same direction as the weight-loss difference. The investigators' own framing is that both are effective and surgery gives the greater long-term risk reduction, particularly where weight loss is larger and better sustained.
practical: The endpoint is a RISK SCORE, not an event. This study measured one-year changes in ASCVD risk-calculator output in a retrospective cohort — it did not observe myocardial infarctions, strokes or deaths, and a modelled lifetime risk reduction is a projection built on the assumption that the weight loss persists. That assumption is the substance of the comparison: GLP-1 therapy stops working when it stops, and adherence and discontinuation rates in practice are high. Present this to a patient as evidence that surgery produces larger and more durable weight loss with correspondingly larger projected risk reduction, not as evidence that surgery prevents more heart attacks than a GLP-1 — no trial has shown that.
link: Mayo Clinic — bariatric surgery versus GLP-1 therapy and projected cardiovascular risk

verify.status: corrected — figures exact, but a modelled risk score was presented as a cardiovascular outcome
verify.note: Verified: Ghusn et al., Annals of Surgery, published 20 April 2026, 812 patients (579 MBS, 233 GLP-1 RA), lifetime ASCVD risk reduction 8.6% versus 1.7%, weight loss 28% versus 11%. Every number in the submission matches. The correction is about what was measured. This is a RETROSPECTIVE COHORT of one-year change in ESTIMATED 10-year and lifetime ASCVD risk — a risk-calculator projection, not observed cardiovascular events. The submission's conclusion, that this 'reframes bariatric surgery... as a primary disease-modifying cardiovascular intervention SUPERIOR to long-term GLP-1 monotherapy', overstates a risk-score comparison into a demonstrated outcome superiority, and the investigators' own quoted framing is more measured ('both treatments are effective, but surgery appears to provide a greater reduction'). Entry rewritten to say so, with the durability assumption — which is what the lifetime projection rests on — made explicit.

title: MAPLE-PD: Mesenteric (Artery-First) Versus Conventional Pancreatoduodenectomy
breakthrough: MAPLE-PD randomised patients with resectable or borderline-resectable (portal vein involvement) pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma at 24 Japanese high-volume centres to an infracolic SMA-first mesenteric approach or the conventional Kocher-first approach. Median overall survival was 41.7 months with the conventional approach and 39.3 months with the mesenteric approach — comparable, HR 1.02 (95% CI 0.76–1.37), P=0.897 by intention to treat; one-year survival 86.1% versus 82.3% and two-year 70.8% versus 66.6%. A circulating tumour cell substudy did show what the approach was designed to do: mean change in CTC DNA copy number in portal vein blood between laparotomy and specimen removal was +10.1 conventional versus −7.3 mesenteric (p<0.001).
impact: A well-conducted randomised trial of a technical manoeuvre that is widely taught as oncologically superior, and it is negative for survival. What survives is the mechanistic claim — the no-touch isolation really does reduce intraoperative tumour cell shedding into the portal vein — without that translating into longer life.
practical: The lesson is where the leverage actually is: with lymphadenectomy standardised, procedural sequence did not change survival, so surgical volume, complete R0 margins and delivery of multidisciplinary systemic therapy are what to optimise. Use the artery-first approach where it helps you assess resectability or control the SMA margin in a borderline case — that is a sound intraoperative reason — but do not offer it to a patient as a survival advantage, and do not let a negative trial of one manoeuvre be read as a negative verdict on the no-touch principle, which the CTC data support.
link: MAPLE-PD — mesenteric versus conventional approach during pancreatoduodenectomy for PDAC

verify.status: matched with corrections — direction right, date wrong, and the positive substudy was omitted
verify.note: Verified: MAPLE-PD, Annals of Surgery, 24 Japanese high-volume centres, protocol target 354 patients, median OS 41.7 (conventional) versus 39.3 months (mesenteric), HR 1.02, P=0.897; the trial concluded the mesenteric approach does not improve survival. The submission got the DIRECTION right, which is notable — most submissions in this review overstated. Three corrections: (1) it is a 2025 publication (PubMed 40772617), not 'Annals of Surgery, 2026'; (2) the submission omits the CTC substudy, which is the trial's positive finding and the reason the no-touch rationale is not refuted — worth including precisely because it stops the entry reading as 'artery-first is pointless'; (3) 'resectable/borderline' is specified in the trial as borderline by PORTAL VEIN involvement (BR-PV), not borderline by arterial abutment, which is a different and more difficult group. The submission's own inference — that volume, systemic therapy and R0 outweigh procedural sequence — is the trial authors' conclusion and has been kept.

title: Treatment Delay Thresholds and Metastasis Risk in Colorectal Cancer
breakthrough: A cohort study of 11,927 insured patients with nonmetastatic colorectal cancer used machine learning to look for time-to-treatment-initiation thresholds beyond which three-year systemic metastasis risk rises, analysing four care pathways separately: surgery alone, neoadjuvant then surgery, surgery then adjuvant therapy, and trimodality therapy. In the surgery-then-adjuvant pathway, starting treatment 4–46 days after diagnosis carried a 27% higher metastasis risk than starting within 3 days, rising to 55% higher beyond 46 days. The thresholds differed by pathway rather than following a single deadline.
impact: It argues against the arbitrary uniform 30-day target and for pathway-specific timelines, and it puts a number on the cost of administrative drift between diagnosis and treatment.
practical: Read the reference group before acting on the 27%. That figure compares everything from day 4 onward against treatment started within THREE DAYS of diagnosis — a window almost no elective colorectal pathway can meet, and one that in a real cohort is largely occupied by patients presenting acutely with obstruction or perforation who go straight to theatre. Treating "beyond 4 days" as a harm threshold would be a misreading, and pursuing it would mean operating before staging is complete. The defensible use of this study is the upper threshold — delay past about six to seven weeks is where risk climbs steeply — and its actual message, which is that the deadline that matters depends on which pathway the patient is on. This is a retrospective claims-based cohort in an insured population, so residual confounding by acuity and comorbidity is unresolved.
link: Colorectal cancer treatment delay thresholds and metastasis risk

verify.status: corrected — journal wrong, and the '4 days' threshold is a misread reference group that would drive unsafe practice
verify.note: SAFETY-RELEVANT FRAMING. The study is real: Nguyen et al., cohort of 11,927 insured patients with nonmetastatic colorectal cancer, machine-learning TTI thresholds across four treatment pathways. Corrections. (1) Journal: JAMA NETWORK OPEN, not JAMA Surgery as submitted. (2) The submission states 'treatment delays beyond 4 days were associated with a 27% increase in metastasis'. The published comparison is initiation at 4–46 days versus WITHIN 3 DAYS — the 27% is relative to a three-day reference, not a harm threshold at day 4. Presented as submitted, a reader would conclude that a colorectal cancer must be treated within four days of diagnosis, which is not achievable in an elective pathway, would preclude complete staging and multidisciplinary discussion, and would be actively worse care. The reference group in a real cohort is dominated by acute obstructive/perforated presentations, which is a confounder, not a target. (3) '55% if delays exceeded 47 days' is approximately right (beyond 46 days) and has been retained as the usable finding. (4) The submission's 'Multi-Cohort Pathway Threshold Study' framing obscures that this is retrospective claims data in an insured population; stated plainly.

title: E-AHPBA–ESSO–Innsbruck Consensus on Peri- and Postoperative Management After Liver Resection
breakthrough: A European consensus developed by hepatobiliary surgeons, anaesthetists, hepatologists, a nurse and a physiotherapist used a modified Delphi process with a 70% agreement threshold to produce 32 statements across six topics: thromboprophylaxis, antibiotics, prehabilitation–nutrition–mobilisation, bile leaks including bilio-enteric anastomosis, post-hepatectomy haemorrhage, and post-hepatectomy liver failure. Screening reduced 6,514 publications to 204 included; the median evidence level of the statements was 2. Strong recommendations were formulated for prehabilitation, early postoperative mobilisation and AVOIDANCE OF ROUTINE DRAIN USE; the weakest evidence was found for perioperative thromboprophylaxis and for management of post-hepatectomy liver failure.
impact: It replaces heterogeneous local protocols with one European framework, and it is honest about where the evidence runs out — naming thromboprophylaxis and post-hepatectomy liver failure as the two areas where practice is running ahead of data and multicentre studies are needed.
practical: The three strong recommendations are the ones to act on, and one of them is a deprescribing decision: do not place a drain routinely after liver resection. Prehabilitation and early mobilisation are cheap, unglamorous and the best-supported items in the document. Where a statement rests on level-2 evidence with 70% panel agreement — which is most of them — it is guidance for standardisation, not a standard of care to be audited against.
link: E-AHPBA–ESSO–Innsbruck consensus recommendations on peri- and postoperative management following liver resection

verify.status: corrected — right document, wrong recommendations attributed to it
verify.note: The document is real and correctly cited: BJS January 2026, volume 113 issue 1, znaf272, E-AHPBA–ESSO–Innsbruck consensus. The problem is the content. The submission lists the key directives as 'parenchyma-sparing strategies, routine intraoperative ultrasound navigation, strict fluid restriction to maintain low central venous pressure (CVP), and early postoperative mobilization', and frames the scope as standardised guidelines for open and minimally invasive hepatectomy. The published consensus covers PERI- AND POSTOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT — thromboprophylaxis, antibiotics, prehabilitation/nutrition/mobilisation, bile leaks, post-hepatectomy haemorrhage and PHLF — not operative technique; parenchyma-sparing resection, intraoperative ultrasound and low-CVP anaesthesia are not among its topics. Only 'early postoperative mobilisation' from the submitted list is actually in it. Its three STRONG recommendations are prehabilitation, early mobilisation and avoidance of routine drains, and the last of those — a directly actionable deprescribing recommendation — was missing from the submission entirely. Entry rewritten to the document's real content, including its stated evidence limits.

title: PSOGI Consensus on Minimally Invasive Surgery for Peritoneal Surface Malignancy
breakthrough: The Peritoneal Surface Oncology Group International published consensus recommendations on minimally invasive — laparoscopic and robotic — surgery for peritoneal surface malignancy, covering selection criteria for minimally invasive cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy and the diagnostic and staging roles of laparoscopy. Where evidence was insufficient the panel recorded no agreement rather than manufacturing one: for low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm type II lesions there was no consensus that surgery is preferable to observation, though if surgery is undertaken it should include resection of the appendiceal stump and the right iliac fossa peritoneum.
impact: Minimally invasive cytoreduction has been spreading ahead of any evidence base. Restricting it to carefully selected low-Peritoneal-Cancer-Index disease at expert centres puts a boundary on adoption before the technique is applied to burdens of disease it cannot clear.
practical: The governing principle in cytoreductive surgery is completeness of cytoreduction — an incomplete resection through a laparoscopic approach is worse than an open complete one, and there is no partial credit. Low PCI, expert centre, and a firm intention to convert are the conditions. Note also that this consensus is as useful for what it refuses to recommend: 'no agreement' on operating versus observing a LAMN II is a legitimate answer to take into a clinic, not a gap to fill with local preference.
link: PSOGI consensus on minimally invasive surgery for peritoneal surface malignancy

verify.status: matched with corrections — document confirmed, scope broader than submitted
verify.note: Confirmed: 'PSOGI consensus on minimally invasive surgery for peritoneal surface malignancy', BJS volume 113 issue 3, znag019 — matching the submission's British Journal of Surgery, March 2026 attribution. Corrections: (1) the scope is minimally invasive surgery for peritoneal surface malignancy broadly, including diagnostic/staging laparoscopy and appendiceal neoplasms, not solely 'minimally invasive CRS + HIPEC' as submitted; (2) the submission's specifics — 'restricts to highly selected patients with low PCI scores performed at expert centers, establishing safety benchmarks' — are directionally consistent with the consensus's purpose but the exact PCI thresholds could not be verified from accessible sources, so they are stated qualitatively rather than numerically. Added the LAMN II no-agreement statement, which is verifiable and clinically useful, and the completeness-of-cytoreduction principle that governs whether a minimally invasive approach is appropriate at all.

title: SAGES 2026: Video-Based Assessment and Opioid-Sparing Perioperative Care
breakthrough: Two threads from the SAGES 2026 meeting in Tampa. The SAGES Artificial Intelligence Committee presented a surgical gesture ontology — a universal, instrument-agnostic framework for defining and annotating surgical gestures across procedures, built for deployment in large-scale video-based assessment — alongside programming on video-based skill assessment for surgeon performance. Separately, SAGES updated its OpiVoid CME activity, an evidence-based programme on opioid-sparing perioperative care that also satisfies the DEA MATE Act education requirement.
impact: Video-based assessment is the first plausible route to objective, scalable feedback on operative technique, and an agreed annotation ontology is the unglamorous prerequisite — without shared definitions of what a gesture is, no two institutions' AI assessments are comparable. On the analgesia side, multimodal opioid-sparing regimens within ERAS are established practice; the contribution here is structured education rather than new evidence.
practical: Treat both as directions of travel, not requirements. There is no SAGES practice directive mandating opioid-free anaesthesia and no accreditation pathway built on AI video assessment — a gesture ontology is infrastructure, and OpiVoid is a CME course. If your unit is recording operative video for assessment, the governance questions (consent, retention, who can view a named surgeon's score, and whether it becomes a credentialling instrument) need answering before the technology arrives, not after.
link: SAGES 2026 — video-based assessment for surgical skill

verify.status: corrected — conference programming and a CME course were presented as practice directives
verify.note: The underlying activity is real: SAGES 2026 Annual Meeting, Tampa Convention Center, 25–28 March 2026, with video-based assessment programming, an AI Committee surgical gesture ontology, and an updated OpiVoid CME activity announced October 2025 covering the DEA MATE Act requirement. The submission's framing is what needed correcting: it cites 'SAGES Practice Directives & Tech Consensus' and describes 'AI video-based assessment (VBA) for intraoperative skill ACCREDITATION' and 'widespread implementation' of opioid-free anaesthesia as if a guideline had been issued. No SAGES practice directive on opioid-free anaesthesia and no VBA-based accreditation pathway could be found; a gesture ontology is annotation infrastructure and OpiVoid is a CME course. The submission's outcome claims — accelerated bowel function recovery, discharge readiness, objective automated feedback on critical-view-of-safety compliance — are aspirations of the programme, not measured results, and 'critical view of safety' compliance assessment specifically could not be sourced to SAGES 2026 at all. Entry rewritten as a direction-of-travel item with the governance question added, since that is what a unit actually has to decide.

title: Remote Perioperative Telemonitoring in Cancer Surgery
breakthrough: A randomised trial assigned 293 patients undergoing gastrointestinal, genitourinary or gynaecological cancer surgery to remote perioperative monitoring or surgeon-only care. The monitored arm wore a wristband accelerometer and reported symptoms through an app before surgery and at days 7, 14, 30, 60 and 90 after discharge, with triage nurses telephoning when data crossed predetermined thresholds. Functional recovery rate was 6% greater in the monitored arm (p=0.036); symptom severity differed significantly at day 90 and symptom interference with daily activities at days 14 and 90, both favouring monitoring.
impact: It establishes a modest but real benefit for structured post-discharge monitoring in cancer surgery, and it identifies the active ingredient: the earlier feasibility work found adherence depended on the nurse-supported arm, where patients received a phone call when data were missing. The technology is the sensor; the intervention is the person who rings.
practical: Six per cent on functional recovery is worth having and is not a transformation — set expectations accordingly before buying a platform. The trial did not demonstrate early detection of anastomotic leak, a reduction in 30-day readmissions, or shortened time to adjuvant therapy; those remain plausible mechanisms, not findings. Before implementing, decide who is monitoring the alerts out of hours and what the escalation pathway is: an unread threshold breach is worse than no monitoring, because it creates a record that a deterioration was flagged and not acted on.
link: Comparative effectiveness of remote perioperative telemonitoring in cancer surgery: a randomized trial

verify.status: NOT FOUND as cited — journal, year and every claimed outcome differ from the real trial
verify.note: No Annals of Surgery January 2026 prospective digital health trial of this description could be found. The real randomised evidence is Sun et al., npj Digital Medicine 8:555 (2025), 293 patients with GI/GU/GYN cancer, wristband accelerometer plus app symptom reporting with nurse triage — its result is a 6% greater functional recovery rate (p=0.036) plus symptom severity and interference differences at days 14 and 90. The submission's claimed outcomes are NOT findings of any located trial: 'early detection of subtle infectious complications (e.g. anastomotic leaks, pelvic abscesses) before overt clinical collapse', 'a significant drop in 30-day unplanned readmissions', and 'shortened time-to-adjuvant chemotherapy initiation'. The earlier World Journal of Surgery 2023 RCT in GI oncologic surgery was a FEASIBILITY and ACCEPTABILITY study and reported no such outcomes either. Entry rewritten to the real trial and its real effect size, with the unsupported outcomes explicitly marked as mechanisms rather than results, and the operational prerequisite the submission omitted — who answers the alert — added.

title: EHS/AHS Guideline on Abdominal Wall Closure: Small Bites and Prophylactic Mesh
breakthrough: The joint European and American Hernia Societies guideline on closure of abdominal wall incisions recommends, for elective midline laparotomy, a continuous small-bites technique with a suture-to-wound-length ratio of at least 4:1, using a slowly absorbable monofilament in a single-layer aponeurotic closure without separate peritoneal closure, and avoiding rapidly absorbable sutures. Small bites means tissue bites of 5–9 mm taking aponeurosis only, with stitches 5 mm apart. Prophylactic mesh augmentation is judged effective and safe and is suggested for high-risk patients — abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery and obesity are the named groups.
impact: It converts closure from a matter of individual habit into a specified technique with a measurable target. The evidence base is the STITCH randomised trial, which compared small bites against large bites for midline closure and found fewer incisional hernias at one year in the small-bites arm.
practical: The 4:1 ratio is the checkable part — it means roughly four times as much suture as wound length, which in practice is far more stitches than most closures use, and a surgeon who believes they already close with small bites usually is not. Count it once against a measured wound to calibrate. The technique takes longer, and that is the trade. For prophylactic mesh, the recommendation is 'suggested in high-risk patients', a conditional recommendation — not routine, and emergency laparotomy is a separate question with its own trials still reporting.
link: Updated guideline for closure of abdominal wall incisions from the European and American Hernia Societies

verify.status: corrected — content accurate but this is a 2022 guideline, not a 2026 development, and the effect size is overstated
verify.note: The clinical content is right and matches the published guideline: continuous small bites, 4:1 suture-to-wound-length ratio, slowly absorbable monofilament single-layer aponeurotic closure, prophylactic mesh suggested in high-risk patients including AAA surgery and obesity. Two corrections. (1) DATE: the submission presents this as a 2026 BJS publication ('EHS & AHS Joint Directives', no date given, listed as a 2026 development). The current joint EHS/AHS guideline is BJS 2022, volume 109, pages 1239ff, building on the 2015 EHS guideline — there is no 2026 replacement, so this belongs in the list as established standard rather than a new advance. (2) EFFECT SIZE: the submission claims small bites 'reduces 2-year incisional hernia rates by up to 50% compared to traditional large-bite closure'. The STITCH trial's result is at ONE year and smaller than that; no 2-year 50% reduction could be sourced. Replaced with a statement of what STITCH showed without a fabricated percentage. Added the technical definition (5–9 mm bites, 5 mm apart) and the observation that the ratio is checkable, since a directive nobody can audit changes nothing, and flagged that prophylactic mesh is a CONDITIONAL recommendation, not routine.
